sentences.text: Stenonychosaurus is a disputed genus of troodontid dinosaur, a name meaning "narrow claw lizard," originally named by Charles Mortram Sternberg in 1932.
This small creature stood about 0.9 meters tall and measured between 2.4 and 3.5 meters in length.
It possessed one of the largest known brains relative to body mass among dinosaurs, comparable to modern birds.
A notable feature of the remains was an enlarged claw on the second toe, a trait now recognized as characteristic of early paravian dinosaurs.
The species was originally described based on foot, hand fragments, and tail vertebrae from the Late Cretaceous of Alberta.
A more complete skeleton was later described by Dale Russell in 1969, forming the basis for a famous life-sized sculpture.
Stenonychosaurus is believed to have been a predator, supported by its sickle-shaped toe claw, though a comparative study of the feeding apparatus suggests it may have been an omnivore.
The dinosaur possessed semi-manipulative fingers capable of grasping objects and binocular vision.
It possessed very long, slender hind limbs that suggest it was capable of running quickly.
The dinosaur had bony cristae supporting its tympanic membranes, which were ossified in at least the top and bottom regions.
The jaws of Stenonychosaurus met in a broad, U-shaped symphysis similar to that of an iguana adapted to a plant-eating lifestyle.
Growth ring counts suggest that Stenonychosaurus reached its adult size in approximately 3 to 5 years.
A partial skeleton with preserved bite marks, possibly inflicted by a predator, has been discovered.
Historically, Stenonychosaurus was grouped with Saurornithoides in the family Saurornithoididae.
Sternberg initially classified Stenonychosaurus as a member of the family Coeluridae.

A 2021 analysis determined that characters previously diagnostic of Latenivenatrix were actually individual variables, the two taxa overlap stratigraphically, and Latenivenatrix mcmasterae is a junior synonym of Stenonychosaurus inequalis.
Stenonychosaurus lived during the late Upper Cretaceous, approximately 76 million years ago in the Campanian stage, in what is now North America.
It became a very well-known theropod in the 1980s when its feet and cranial box were described in more detail.
It is debated whether the evolutionary trajectory of Stenonychosaurus would have led to human-like intelligence, with critics arguing such a scenario is overly anthropomorphic.
A later analysis found that the type of parental care in troodonts cannot be determined using the conventional allometric methods used by Varricchio et al.
Stenonychosaurus inequalis was reassigned as a synonym of the genus Troodon in 1987 by Philip J. Currie, a decision later reversed by Evans et al. and Van der Reest and Currie in the same year.
In 2011, Zanno and colleagues noted that numerous specimens currently assigned to Troodon formosus likely represent many new species, though a more exhaustive review of the specimens is required.
